title: Require a documented GDPR legal basis and age-verification before launching a consumer AI product to EU users
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on the Italian Garante's enforcement actions against ChatGPT and Replika. Not a documented decision of any specific organization.

history.note: Initial Phase 2A seed content, part of the Foundational Twenty.

Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources). Normalized a duplicated relationship-reason phrasing ("...via this design pattern." -> "...via this single, primary design pattern.") to one canonical wording.

decision_statement: Before a consumer-facing AI product processes EU users' personal data, the organization must document its GDPR legal basis for that processing (including for any training data drawn from user interactions), publish a clear privacy notice, and implement an effective age-verification mechanism where the product could plausibly be used by minors.
decision_context: Motivated by two Italian Garante enforcement actions in early 2023 — against ChatGPT and against the AI companion app Replika — both citing an inadequate GDPR legal basis and ineffective age verification.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Consumer AI Product Governance Board
alternatives_considered: Launch first in the EU and address legal-basis documentation reactively if a regulator raises concerns.
Rely on terms-of-service age restrictions without a technical verification mechanism.

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this enforcement action.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern.
A documented legal basis and privacy notice satisfy this control's core data-processing principles.
Compliance is demonstrated by the same data protection impact assessment used for other GDPR-triggering processing.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether age verification is effective, not merely present in terms of service.
